title: The rose-apple tree
hook: at the plowing festival the boy sits in the shade and falls into a quiet joy (MN 36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Siddhattha, the one whose aim succeeds, and Kondañña's single raised finger. A name is a wish.

The plowing festival. The whole town is out in the fields: music, food, bright clothes, oxen with decorated horns, and the king himself takes hold of a golden plow to open the season. Everyone watches the king. Nobody watches the boy. His nurses have set him down in the shade of a rose-apple tree at the edge of the field and wandered off to see the show. Alone, the boy sits cross-legged, quiet. And something happens that he'll remember for the rest of his life.
screen: `THE PLOWING FESTIVAL.` → `EVERYONE WATCHES THE KING.` → `A BOY UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: The festival details come from later tellings, but the heart of this story is the Buddha's own, from a discourse where he looks back on his search. He's describing the punishing practices of those years, the fasting and the strain, and how they got him nowhere. At his lowest point, he remembers: when his father was working in the fields, he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree and entered a quiet joy, secluded from wanting, secluded from anything unwholesome, with a happiness born of that seclusion. He calls it the first jhana. Could that be the way to awakening? he wonders, and realizes it is. Then comes the question that turns his whole search around: why am I afraid of that kind of happiness, one that has nothing to do with the pleasures of the senses? Jhana means deep meditative absorption: the mind settling, gathering, becoming still and bright. The texts describe four levels, each quieter than the last. And a surprise: the Pali jhana is dhyana in Sanskrit. When Buddhism reached China, dhyana became chan. In Japan, chan became zen. The name Zen comes from this word. For the Buddha, the point wasn't the joy itself. It was the memory. Peace wasn't something he had to force, starve for or conquer. He'd found it by himself, as a child, doing nothing, in the shade.
screen: `THE BUDDHA REMEMBERS THE TREE.` · `THE FIRST JHANA: A QUIET JOY.` · `WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT HAPPINESS?` · `JHANA, DHYANA, CHAN, ZEN.` · then, large: `YOU'VE BEEN HERE BEFORE.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit somewhere shady: under a tree, by a window, in a quiet corner. Do nothing, not even meditating, exactly; be still the way a child is when nobody's watching, and let the breath do what it does. If a little ease shows up, a small quiet pleasure in simply being here, don't be afraid of it: let it stay.
Jhana. Meditative absorption: the mind gathered, still and bright. Dhyana in Sanskrit, the root of chan and zen.
Your line: you've been here before. Peace came first to a child in the shade. Day twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhists develop jhana through concentration meditation, often on the breath; it is taught in Theravada meditation traditions as the four absorptions, and the word itself, through Sanskrit dhyana and Chinese chan, gave Zen its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice memory from childhood.
what it means: the Buddha's memory of the first jhana under a rose-apple tree, which showed him that peace comes by letting go, not by force.

what a scholar hears: in the Mahasaccaka Sutta (MN 36) the Buddha recalls the first jhāna and asks why he fears a pleasure apart from the senses. the plowing festival setting comes from the Nidanakatha.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the memory under the rose-apple tree

notes: MN 36 paraphrased: 'while my Sakyan father was working' (some translations: 'occupied'), the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, the first jhana, 'could this be the path?', 'why am I afraid of that pleasure?'. Chalmers's 1926 translation is not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted. Confirm.
The festival details (golden plow, nurses wandering off, the tree's shadow not moving) are from the Nidanakatha; the script mentions only the setting. Confirm.
jhana > dhyana > chan > zen: the standard etymology; confirm.
Four jhanas mentioned briefly; the formless attainments are not taught here.
